lines.text: South of the Corrow lands, the world turned warm. Vineyards. Orchards. Roses still blooming at the end of autumn. Ash didn't trust any of it.
But every morning there was frost on the vines. Just a little. The farmers scraped it off and swore it had never come this far south before.
The old chronicles say that while King Aldric lived, the south never saw frost at all. It's been creeping closer ever since.
We reached Aldcrown on the ninth morning. White walls, gold roofs, a hundred towers, and above them all, the seven spires of the Cathedral of the Seven.
Oswin had warned me it was big. He hadn't warned me it would smell like ten thousand people and one river.
Name, and rings?
Lucan Varr. Zero.
The zero? The King's zero? Ha! Lads, it's the zero! ...Is that a dog?
Inside the gates, the Highmarket glittered with silk and glass. And everywhere, young lords strolled about with five rings stitched in gold on their sleeves.
When I was a girl, there were forty true lords in all of Aldmere. I've counted eleven five-ring heirs since the gate. Rings don't multiply like that, Lucan.
Mine do.
That is exactly what worries me.
Below the walls was the Lowmarket. Crooked houses piled on each other, mud streets, and a long line of people waiting at a single well.
Above it, an old aqueduct marched across the valley on tall stone legs. Halfway across, one arch had fallen, and the channel above it was dry.
I noticed it the way you notice a crooked picture. I told myself it wasn't my problem.
We took rooms at a crooked inn that Oswin swore was respectable. It wasn't. Ash liked it immediately.
That evening, Tamsin went up to the Order's College to report, like a good little Measurer, with a forged report and a very brave face.
The next morning, I walked to the cathedral with Ash. The place where Aldric lit seven. The place where they would put my hand on a Stone again.
Somewhere beneath it, in the dark, a woman was humming a song I knew. I didn't know that then. I only felt cold on the steps, and didn't know why.
At the top of the stair, a man in white robes was watching me. Short white hair. A kind, tired face.
I had never seen him before. But I knew him the way you know a wolf you've only ever heard at night.
Grand Measurer Aurel Vance smiled at me, like an old friend. And waved.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter seventy-one, coming soon.
